title: Acts, looking back
hookLine: wind, fire, a road, a shipwreck, and a door left open in Rome
tomorrow: six practices. which one actually stayed?
last: THE WEEK THAT TURNED THE WORLD.

cards: Some things only reach you by hand: a recipe card in a grandmother's writing, a song a friend once played you in the car, a joke that's been through six group chats.
Acts is the story of how a story from one garden in Jerusalem traveled. Wind, fire, a road, a shipwreck, and a door left open in Rome.

teach.b: Before he's taken up, Jesus gives a map: “ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.”
Acts follows it outward: wind and fire at Pentecost; Saul thrown down on the Damascus road, who becomes Paul and carries the story across the sea; a shipwreck where everyone reaches land; and Rome.
The question underneath: who is the story for? Paul answers in Athens, speaking to people who didn't share his scriptures.
God, he says, “hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth.” One blood. One human family.
Then he does something worth telling a friend: he quotes their own poets back to them, “as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring.” Now a neighbor.

teach.h: A NEIGHBOR: FOR THE WELFARE OF THE MANY.
teach.b: In the Buddhist scriptures, the Buddha sends out his first monks with words that sound close: go and wander “for the gain of the many, for the welfare of the many, out of compassion for the world.”

Shared ground: a teaching not kept in one room, carried on foot, for the good of everyone. An honest difference: the monks carry a path to walk, the Dhamma; the witnesses in Acts carry news of a person, Jesus, risen.
Paul is in Rome under guard, preaching “with all confidence, no man forbidding him,” and the book stops.
The door stays open, hand to hand, to whoever is listening now.

how: Christians read Acts in worship, in some churches especially in the weeks after Easter, and some communities tell how the faith first reached their own town or family.

games.q: a classmate from a Buddhist family says, "my grandma says the Buddha sent his monks out for the welfare of the many. sounds like your Acts." what's a fair reply?
o: they're the same message, just in different words.
yes, both send people out for the good of many; the monks carry a path, Acts carries news of a person.
no, the two have nothing in common at all.
games.why: both send their message out on foot, for everyone. the honest difference: the Buddha's monks carry the Dhamma, a path; the witnesses in Acts carry news of Jesus, risen.

practice: Trace how this story reached you, if it did: a person, a place, a book, a song. Follow the line back as far as it goes and name each hand it passed through.
If one of them is only a text away, send them one line of thanks; if you pray, thank God for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Acts. The book that follows the first witnesses outward from Jerusalem, and ends with Paul in Rome and the door still open.
